questions.subtopic: 2.2 Redundancy. Testing BC and DR plans
questions.question: A tabletop exercise finds two outdated supplier numbers in a cement maker's recovery plan; the IT manager owns the plan, but procedure has the continuity coordinator correct contact details. What should the coordinator do FIRST?

options.A: Report and record both numbers for the IT manager to correct
options.B: Rerun the tabletop to confirm the two numbers are really wrong
options.C: Correct the two numbers in the plan and record the change
options.D: Schedule a full interruption test to find any other errors

questions.key_concept: Plans are updated after every test; when the procedure assigns an update to the practitioner, they make it and record it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the plan and what the procedure assigns to the coordinator.
questions.correct_explanation: Plans must be updated after every test, and contact lists go stale fastest. The procedure gives contact corrections to the continuity coordinator, so they fix both numbers now and record the change in the plan's history. Reporting them for the IT manager to correct is the runner-up: the manager owns the plan, but the procedure already assigns this task to the coordinator, so routing it back only adds delay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the IT manager owns the plan. But the procedure assigns contact corrections to the coordinator, so passing them back only delays a fix that is theirs to make.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because test findings should be sound. But the numbers were already found outdated; rerunning the exercise only delays a simple fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it would test everything. But a full interruption risks a real outage, needs senior management approval and is not how contact errors are fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats an exercise that already found the errors, and D jumps to a disruptive test that needs senior management approval.
Final two: C beats A because the procedure gives contact fixes to the coordinator; owning the plan does not mean doing every update.
Exam cue: when the procedure assigns a task to you, do it and record it, even if someone else owns the document.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.6 (Plan Maintenance: contact lists need more frequent review than other plan elements); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing)

questions.question: At a mobile phone retailer, store managers praise staff who skip the required ID check on account changes to shorten queues, and skipping is now common. What should the security manager propose FIRST?

options.A: Ask senior leaders to join the staff's next ID check training
options.B: Have managers formally warn staff found skipping the check
options.C: Drop the ID check during busy hours to shorten queues
options.D: Ask senior leaders to have managers reward doing the check

questions.key_concept: People repeat what gets rewarded; when managers praise skipping a control, leaders must change what is rewarded before training or discipline can work.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the staff's behavior is coming from.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff skip the check because their managers praise it, so the behavior comes from what local leaders reward, and culture follows what leaders reward. Senior leaders setting the expectation that managers reward doing the check fixes the cause. Senior leaders joining training is the runner-up: a good example helps, but staff already know the rule, and they will keep skipping it while their managers praise the shortcut.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: leaders' example shapes culture. But staff already know the check is required; while their managers praise skipping it, a leader at training will not change behavior.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the check is required. But punishing staff for what their managers reward breeds resentment and hiding, and leaves the cause in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it ends the conflict. But the check stops account takeover; removing it at peak times hands attackers the busiest, least-watched window.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes staff for what their managers reward, and C removes a control to suit the queue.
Final two: D beats A because the shortcut is driven by what managers praise, not a lack of example; change the reward before anything else.
Exam cue: find what drives the behavior. If leaders skip a rule, fix their example; if managers reward a shortcut, fix what they reward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)

questions.question: A vehicle inspection agency's awareness lead wants a low-cost way to keep one habit, locking screens, in every employee's mind all year. Which activity BEST fits this goal?

options.A: A short monthly screen-lock reminder sent to all staff
options.B: A hands-on half-day screen-lock workshop for every team
options.C: A role-based screen-lock course for the IT support staff
options.D: A one-time screen-lock module added to the onboarding course

questions.key_concept: Awareness uses short, frequent messages to keep a simple habit in everyone's mind; training and onboarding modules serve other goals.
questions.pre_read: Match the goal, the audience and the time frame to a kind of learning.
questions.correct_explanation: Keeping one simple habit in everyone's mind all year is an awareness goal, and awareness works through short, frequent messages to all staff at low cost. A monthly reminder fits all three needs. The onboarding module is the runner-up: it reaches every new starter, but a one-time lesson fades, and staff already employed never see it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hands-on practice builds skill. But locking a screen needs no lab; a half-day workshop for everyone costs far more and happens once.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because role-based training targets risk. But this habit is for every employee, not one team, so a course for IT support misses most staff.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: onboarding reaches every new starter. But a one-time lesson fades, and staff already employed never see it, so it cannot keep the habit alive.

tips: Eliminate: B uses costly training for a simple habit, and C aims a role-based course at one team when everyone needs the habit.
Final two: A beats D because awareness must be repeated to last; a one-time onboarding module fades and misses current staff.
Exam cue: everyone, simple and ongoing means awareness; a specific role and skill means training.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.7.1 (Awareness Activities: ongoing, timely messages for all users throughout the year)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Awareness reaches everyone through short, frequent messages, such as reminders and brief campaigns' (notes 2.3.2 Awareness, Training and Education). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a television studio's staff entrance, a stranger who slipped in behind an employee becomes angry and threatening when asked to sign in. What should the employee do FIRST?

options.A: Block the doorway until the stranger shows a staff badge
options.B: Follow the stranger at a safe distance to see where they go
options.C: Firmly ask the stranger again to sign in
options.D: Move away to a safe spot and call building security

questions.key_concept: When a social engineering attempt turns threatening, personal safety comes first: get clear and let trained security staff handle it.
questions.pre_read: Decide what matters most once the stranger becomes threatening.
questions.correct_explanation: Once the stranger turns threatening, the risk is to people, and safety comes before access control. Moving to a safe spot and calling building security protects the employee and brings trained staff to deal with the intruder. Following at a safe distance is the runner-up: it keeps track of the intruder, but it keeps the employee close to a hostile person and delays the call for help.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops the intruder going further. But physically blocking an angry, threatening person invites violence; that job belongs to trained security staff.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: knowing where the intruder goes helps, and the distance feels safe. But it keeps the employee near a hostile person and delays the call that brings trained help.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because signing in is the right rule. But repeating a challenge to someone already threatening can raise the danger; it is time to step back.

tips: Eliminate: A blocks a hostile person physically, and C repeats a challenge that has already provoked threats.
Final two: D beats B because people come first; get clear and call security before tracking anyone.
Exam cue: when people are at risk, the first step protects them; handling the intruder comes after.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.8 (Occupant Emergency Plan (OEP)); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'At a badge door, never let in anyone who cannot badge in, whatever uniform or ID card they show; send them to reception to sign in' (notes 2.3.3 Social Engineering Tactics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Emails to a botanical garden's staff link to a copy of its own staff sign-in page, built to capture usernames and passwords. Which term should the security analyst use to name this attack MOST precisely?

options.A: A credential harvesting attack
options.B: A sender spoofing attack
options.C: A whaling attack
options.D: A business email compromise attack

questions.key_concept: Credential harvesting collects usernames and passwords through a fake sign-in page; spoofing fakes a message's sender details.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the page is built to collect from how the message looks.
questions.correct_explanation: Credential harvesting means collecting usernames and passwords through a fake sign-in page, which is exactly what this copied staff page is built to do. Sender spoofing is the runner-up: phishing emails often fake their sender details, but nothing here says the sender was faked, and spoofing names the disguise, not the page's goal of capturing passwords.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: phishing emails often fake their sender. But spoofing names faked sender details; this attack's defining feature is a fake page that collects passwords.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because whaling is a well-known variant. But whaling targets senior leaders, and these emails go to staff in general.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because business email compromise also tricks staff. But it uses a taken-over or impersonated business account to redirect payments, not a fake sign-in page.

tips: Eliminate: C needs senior leaders as the targets, and D needs a compromised business account steering payments.
Final two: A beats B because the attack's goal is a fake page that captures passwords; spoofing names only a faked sender.
Exam cue: name a phishing attack by its defining feature: who it targets, which channel it uses, or what it collects.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)

questions.subtopic: 2.3 Security awareness. AI-boosted phishing and deepfakes
questions.question: A seed bank's lab technician gets a fluent email, likely AI-written, naming their manager, their dog and a recent team outing, and asking them to open a file. What is the technician's MOST accurate conclusion?

options.A: It is likely genuine, since such personal details are rarely public
options.B: It is unproven, since those details could come from public posts
options.C: It is safe to open once antivirus has scanned the file
options.D: It is malicious, since the email was likely written by AI

questions.key_concept: AI lets attackers gather public details and write personal, fluent lures at scale, so personal details in a message prove research, not identity.
questions.pre_read: Think about where an attacker could find each detail in the email.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools let attackers gather details from social media and company pages and weave them into fluent, personal lures at scale. A manager's name, a pet and a team outing are often posted publicly, so they prove research, not identity. Scanning the file is the runner-up: antivirus helps, but new or link-based payloads can pass it, and a clean scan says nothing about who sent the email.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the details feel private. But managers' names, pets and outings are often posted online, and AI tools can gather them for each target in seconds.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: scanning catches known malware. But new payloads and sign-in links can pass a scan, and a clean result does not show who sent the email.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI-written lures are rising. But many genuine emails are written with AI help; the style proves neither who sent it nor their intent, so the request needs checking.

tips: Eliminate: A reads personal details as a sign of a genuine sender, and D treats AI-style writing as proof of an attack; neither shows who sent it.
Final two: B beats C because the real question is who sent it; a clean antivirus scan says nothing about the sender.
Exam cue: with AI-written lures, personal touches prove research, not identity; judge the request, not the polish.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.9 (Information Security: generative AI may augment attacks such as hacking, malware and phishing); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Generative AI writes fluent, personalized lures in many languages, at scale' (notes 2.3.5 AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A gallery's events coordinator learns that a fitness app they use was breached; their work email password is the app's password with one digit changed. What should the coordinator do FIRST?

options.A: Change the fitness app's password and tell the security team
options.B: Watch the work account closely for signs of misuse before acting
options.C: Change the work password and report the leak to the security team
options.D: Keep the work password, since it differs from the leaked one

questions.key_concept: A leaked password exposes every account that uses it or a close variant: change the work password and report it at once.
questions.pre_read: Think about where attackers will try a leaked password next.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers try leaked passwords, and small variations of them, on other sites at once, so a work password one digit away from the leaked one is exposed too. A new, unique work password closes the gap, and reporting lets the security team check for misuse. Changing the app's password is the runner-up: it reports the leak but leaves the work account open to a near copy.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it reports the leak, and the app needs a new password too. But the work password is a near copy that attackers will try next.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has happened yet. But leaked passwords can be tried within hours, and waiting gives attackers time to get in first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the two passwords are not identical. But attackers try small variations of leaked passwords first, so a one-digit change gives little protection.

tips: Eliminate: B waits while attackers try the leaked password, and D trusts a one-digit difference that attackers try among their first guesses.
Final two: C beats A because both report it, but only C changes the near-copy work password that attackers will try next.
Exam cue: a leak anywhere exposes every account that uses the same password or a close variant; change the work one and report it first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Never share a password, even with IT or a manager, and report any exposure at once' (notes 2.3.6 Password and Passphrase Habits). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: With a harder invoice lure, an orchestra's simulated phishing click rate rose from 4% to 12%, while its report rate rose from 30% to 45%. Which reading should the awareness lead report as MOST accurate?

options.A: Awareness has fallen, though more staff reported the lure
options.B: Reporting improved, though the click rates are not comparable
options.C: The test was unfair, since a lure that hard would trick anyone
options.D: Nothing changed, since the click and report rises cancel out

questions.key_concept: Click rates move with lure difficulty, so two simulations are compared only when their lures are alike; report rate shows whether staff act.
questions.pre_read: Consider what changed between the two tests besides the staff.
questions.correct_explanation: Click rates rise and fall with how hard the lure is, so an easy test and a much harder one cannot be compared like for like. The report rate, the behavior that lets the security team act, rose from 30% to 45% against the harder lure. Reading the clicks as falling awareness is the runner-up: it is the obvious figure and it notes the reporting gain, but it compares unlike tests.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: clicks did triple, and it notes the reporting gain. But the lure was harder, so the two click rates are not comparable and do not show awareness falling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the lure caught more people. But realistic, hard lures are fair practice, since real attackers use them; the results still carry meaning.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the figures moved together. But they measure different things; more staff reported, which is the outcome the program most needs.

tips: Eliminate: C throws out a fair, realistic test, and D treats two different behaviors as if they cancel.
Final two: B beats A because click rates track lure difficulty, so these two cannot be compared; reporting is the behavior that shows the program working.
Exam cue: before comparing two simulation results, check the lures were of similar difficulty; a harder lure raises clicks without any change in staff.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.2 (Characteristics of Measures: consistency, time-based reference and replicability); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(1) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Practical Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Track how many people report and how fast, not just how many click' (notes 2.3.7 Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bike-sharing scheme's firewall blocked 2 million attacks this quarter, up from 1.5 million. What should the security manager tell the board this rise MOST accurately shows?

options.A: That more traffic was stopped, which says little about the risk
options.B: That the firewall now protects the scheme better than before
options.C: That the scheme's risk rose by a third and needs treatment
options.D: That the firewall is overloaded and should be replaced soon

questions.key_concept: Raw counts like attacks blocked mostly reflect how often attackers try, so they say little about whether risk is rising or falling.
questions.pre_read: Think about what drives the number of blocked attempts up or down.
questions.correct_explanation: A count of blocked attacks shows only that more traffic was stopped. It rises and falls mostly with how often attackers try, and also with rule or logging changes, so it says little about whether risk is rising or falling. Reading it as better protection is the runner-up: blocks did increase, but the same rules block more whenever more attempts arrive.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firewall did block more. But the same rules block more whenever more attempts arrive, so a higher count does not show better protection.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more attacks sounds like more danger. But the count mostly tracks how often attackers try; risk depends on likelihood and impact, and every attempt was blocked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because volume rose. But nothing in the count shows strain; a firewall that blocks every attempt is doing its job, whatever the volume.

tips: Eliminate: C reads a count of attempts as a measure of risk, and D reads a capacity problem into a simple count.
Final two: A beats B because the same rules block more when more attempts arrive; a higher count does not show better protection.
Exam cue: a count of attacks blocked tracks how hard attackers knock, not how well you defend; ask what drives a number before reading it as progress.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A useful metric ties to a goal, has a target and changes a decision. Raw counts such as "attacks blocked" rarely do' (notes 2.4.1 Measures and Metrics: The Basics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A printing cooperative's IT lead needs an effectiveness measure that shows whether its backups actually work. Which measure BEST fits?

options.A: Share of servers that have the backup software agent installed
options.B: Share of nightly backup jobs that report success
options.C: Average hours each nightly backup job takes to run
options.D: Share of sample restores that return complete, usable data

questions.key_concept: Effectiveness measures show whether a control achieves its purpose; for backups, that means successful test restores.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a backup is ultimately for, then which measure shows that.
questions.correct_explanation: An effectiveness measure shows whether a control achieves its purpose, and a backup's purpose is getting data back. The share of sample restores that return complete, usable data measures that directly. Jobs reporting success is the runner-up: it looks like proof, but a successful job shows only that data was copied, and corrupt or incomplete copies show up only when someone restores them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because coverage matters. But an installed agent shows the control exists, an implementation measure, not that backups can be restored.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: success messages look like proof. But a job can succeed while copying corrupt or incomplete data; only a restore shows it works.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because speed matters. But job run time is an efficiency measure of how fast backups run, not whether they can be restored.

tips: Eliminate: A shows the control is installed, an implementation measure, and C shows how fast jobs run, an efficiency measure.
Final two: D beats B because a job can report success while copying bad data; only restores show the backups work.
Exam cue: for effectiveness, measure the outcome the control exists for, not that it runs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3 (Types of Measures: implementation, effectiveness, efficiency and impact); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-9(1) (System Backup | Testing for Reliability and Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Existence is not effectiveness. To show a control works, use an effectiveness measure' (notes 2.4.2 Types of Security Measures). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: IT judges a college's laptop encryption rate against a 99% rollout target, and the risk owner watches the same rate against a lost-device tolerance. In the risk owner's use, what is it MOST accurately?

options.A: A key performance indicator for the encryption rollout
options.B: A risk tolerance the board has set for lost devices
options.C: A key risk indicator for lost-device data exposure
options.D: An impact measure of what lost devices cost the college

questions.key_concept: The same number can be a KPI or a KRI: it depends on whether it judges a goal or warns a risk nears its limit.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each person compares the figure with.
questions.correct_explanation: A figure works as a key risk indicator when it is watched against a risk's tolerance to warn of growing exposure, which is how the risk owner uses the encryption rate. Calling it a KPI is the runner-up: that is exactly how IT uses it, against the rollout target, but the same number serves a different purpose for the risk owner. What matters is whether it judges performance or warns of risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: for IT it is a KPI against the rollout target. But the risk owner watches it against a tolerance, which makes it a warning of risk, a KRI.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a tolerance is involved. But the tolerance is the limit the figure is compared with; the encryption rate itself is the indicator.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because lost devices cost money. But an impact measure states business cost; an encryption rate shows exposure, not what losses cost.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses the figure with the limit it is compared against, and D calls a coverage rate a cost measure.
Final two: C beats A because the risk owner compares the rate with a tolerance to warn of exposure; for IT, the same number is a KPI.
Exam cue: ask what a number is compared with: a goal makes it a KPI, a risk tolerance makes it a KRI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The same number can be either; what matters is whether it judges performance or warns of risk' (notes 2.4.3 Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A planetarium's indicator for admin accounts lacking MFA turns amber; the security manager owns the risk, but band rules have the access analyst open a fix ticket at amber. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Send the security manager a ticket to decide on a fix
options.B: Move the amber line up until the indicator reads green
options.C: Raise the fix ticket for the admin accounts lacking MFA
options.D: Recheck the admin accounts daily until the band turns red

questions.key_concept: Each threshold band names an action and an owner; when the rule assigns the amber action to the practitioner, they take it without waiting.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the band rules assign at amber, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Thresholds turn numbers into action: each band names what happens and who does it. At amber, the rules give the access analyst the job of raising the fix ticket, so they do it now. Sending it to the security manager is the runner-up: the manager owns the risk, but the rules already assign the amber step to the analyst, so routing it upward only adds delay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the security manager owns the risk. But the band rules assign the amber action to the analyst; asking the owner to decide it delays a step already assigned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because green looks better. But moving a threshold hides the risk without reducing it, and only the threshold's owner may change it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because amber is not yet red. But each band names its own action; waiting for red skips the amber step meant to stop the rise.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the line instead of reducing the risk, and D waits for red when the amber band already names an action.
Final two: C beats A because the band rules give the amber action to the analyst; owning the risk does not mean taking every step.
Exam cue: when a threshold rule assigns an action to your role, take it; escalate only what the rule sends upward.

questions.question: A paper mill's quarterly security report to leaders lists 12 metrics with no commentary, and leaders ask what they are expected to do. Which addition is BEST for the security manager to make?

options.A: A short section on causes and the decisions leaders face
options.B: A color-coded status showing each metric against its target
options.C: A link to the live dashboard so leaders can drill down
options.D: An appendix holding the raw data behind every metric

questions.key_concept: Reports for leaders explain causes and state the decisions needed; status grids, live dashboards and raw data serve other needs.
questions.pre_read: Consider what the leaders asked for, and which format delivers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaders asked what they need to do, and a report's strength is context, causes and recommendations. A short section explaining what drives the results and naming the decisions needed answers them directly. Color-coded status against targets is the runner-up: it shows at a glance which metrics are off track, but not why, or what the leaders should decide.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: status at a glance helps leaders spot problems. But it shows which metrics are off track, not why, or what decision leaders must make.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drill-down shows everything. But live dashboards suit teams acting daily; leaders need conclusions and decisions, not more charts to explore.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it supports transparency. But raw data adds detail, not meaning; it leaves leaders to work out the causes and decisions themselves.

tips: Eliminate: C hands leaders an operations tool, and D adds raw detail; neither tells them what to decide.
Final two: A beats B because leaders asked what to do; color-coded status shows what is off track, not the decisions needed.
Exam cue: match the format to the audience; leaders need causes, trends and decisions, operators need live detail.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A tram operator's average time to disable leavers' accounts doubled in March after a steady year, and the IT manager urges buying an identity governance tool at once. What should the metrics analyst propose FIRST?

options.A: Find out what drove the March figure up
options.B: Buy the tool, since leaver handling has clearly worsened
options.C: Raise the leaver target so the March figure falls within it
options.D: Drop March from the trend as a one-month outlier

questions.key_concept: Before acting on a metric's sudden change, find out why it moved; the cause decides the right fix.
questions.pre_read: Think about what could make one month's figure jump.
questions.correct_explanation: A sudden change in a metric is a question, not an answer: the March jump could come from a data error, a one-off batch of leavers or a missed HR notice, and each needs a different fix. Finding the cause first means the money goes to the real problem. Buying the tool is the runner-up: it acts quickly, but if bad data or a one-off batch drove March, the spend fixes nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it acts quickly on what looks like a decline. But the cause is unknown; if bad data or a one-off batch drove March, the tool fixes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the figure would look on target. But changing the target to fit a bad month hides the problem and improves nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one month can be noise. But dropping a bad month unexamined hides what may be a real problem; it needs explaining, not deleting.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the target to fit a bad result, and D deletes the bad month instead of explaining it.
Final two: A beats B because the cause decides the fix; buying before knowing why the number moved may spend money on the wrong problem.
Exam cue: when a metric jumps, ask why before acting; check the data and the cause, then choose the fix.

questions.question: A city's AI permit-review assistant has risk indicators for accuracy and input drift, but only its data scientists see them, in their own notebooks. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Add the indicators to the main risk dashboard, each with an owner
options.B: Have the data scientists tell the risk owner when they feel concerned
options.C: Replace the indicators with the assistant's monthly uptime figure
options.D: Keep them with the data scientists, who know the model best

questions.key_concept: AI risk indicators belong in the same dashboards and escalation paths as other risks, with owners and thresholds, not in a specialist's private view.
questions.pre_read: Think about who needs to see an AI risk before anyone can act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks should be managed like other critical risks, so their indicators belong on the main risk dashboard, each with an owner, thresholds and an escalation path, where leaders can see and act on them. Having the data scientists tell the risk owner when concerned is the runner-up: it reaches the owner, but it rests on one team's judgment, with no thresholds or routine view.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it gets news to the risk owner. But it relies on one team's judgment of when to speak, with no thresholds or regular view for leaders.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because uptime is easy to report. But uptime shows the assistant answers, not that its answers are right or its inputs still match training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because they know the model. But AI risks belong with other risks, where leaders see them; keeping them private leaves no one accountable to act.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps accuracy for uptime, which says nothing about answer quality, and D keeps AI risk out of leaders' sight.
Final two: A beats B because indicators on the main dashboard, with owners and thresholds, trigger action by rule, not by one team's judgment.
Exam cue: treat AI risk indicators like any other KRI: visible, owned, thresholded and escalated.
